A law in science is an observation. It is not a theory. It is a fact. Gravity, for example: when you drop an apple, it falls to the ground. No alternative phenomenon under the same circumstances has ever been observed. A scientific law describes what nature does under certain conditions and predicts results so long as those conditions remain the same; scientific theory explains how nature works. Thus we have any number of laws of mathematics (without getting into the philosophical question of whether mathematics itself is intrinsically describing something in nature, that is) and Newton's Laws of Motion, which come down to three straight observations: (1) Shit that isn't moving won't move unless some force acts on it. (2) Force = mass x acceleration (3) Slap one motherfucker in the face and he'll slap you back, i.e. every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

Even then, though, laws are just as subject to falsifiability as theories are. Find an object that suddenly changes its speed without any force at all acting on it, and you have to throw out the first law of motion. Find an object that delivers twice as much force as its mass times its acceleration, and you have to throw out the second law. Find a motherfucker who punches you back harder than you punched him, and the third law is thrown out as well. You get the idea.

This is why you've got a lot more laws in chemistry and physics than in biology, or, Christ help us, psychology.
